prompt.context: The maker of Botox is considering expanding to the migraine market and has already begun clinical trials in this area. The product is expected to receive FDA approval in 2016. Your team has been hired to assess the viability of this product for launch.
prompt.question: How will you determine if the market is attractive? If the market is attractive, do you have any recommendations regarding how to launch the product? What concerns should the client take into consideration before deciding to launch? At the conclusion of the case you will need to present your team's recommendation and rationale.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of the drug?
clarifying_info.a: The drug will be priced at $200 per injection.

clarifying_info.q: What are the development and launch costs?
clarifying_info.a: Remaining development and launch costs amount to approximately $5B. Manufacturing marginal costs are expected to be quite small. Annual marketing expense can be estimated at $1B.

clarifying_info.q: How is the drug administered and how often?
clarifying_info.a: It is a prophylactic injection given every 2 months (6 injections per year).

clarifying_info.q: How does this product compare to existing treatments?
clarifying_info.a: It offers similar efficacy compared to the market-leading option but without any side effects. When taken for migraines it does have some added skin care benefits.

clarifying_info.q: What share of migraine sufferers would be willing to try this medicine?
clarifying_info.a: Assume at least 10% of migraine sufferers are willing to try such a medicine (this is a floor; the market sizing uses a broader funnel).
This drug will initially be produced in the US, so the candidate should use US population (300M).

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of the population suffers from migraines?
clarifying_info.a: A reasonable estimate is 20% of the population.

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of migraine sufferers experience severe migraines and would purchase prescription products?
clarifying_info.a: Assume about 50% of chronic migraine sufferers experience severe migraines and are willing to purchase prescription products.

clarifying_info.q: What market share can Botox expect?
clarifying_info.a: Due to the absence of side effects and the beneficial skin care properties, assume 20%-40% of the overall market in 5 years.
The market-leading branded prescription oral migraine treatment lost patent protection last year. There is also a strong over-the-counter generic market for migraine treatments.

framework: 1. Market sizing: Estimate the size of the US prescription migraine market in revenue terms
2. Market attractiveness: Assess whether the revenue opportunity justifies the investment (development, launch, and ongoing marketing costs)
3. Launch considerations: Identify the key strategic challenges and risks associated with launching Botox in a new indication
4. Recommendation: Synthesize findings into a clear go/no-go recommendation with supporting rationale and next steps

questions.prompt: Estimate the total annual US prescription migraine market size in dollars and Botox's potential revenue opportunity.
questions.guidance: A strong candidate walks through each assumption explicitly, labels it as given or estimated, and chains the math cleanly. The key funnel: US population → chronic migraine sufferers → severe sufferers willing to buy prescription products → annual revenue per patient → total market → Botox share.

math.setup: US population x % chronic migraine sufferers x % severe (willing to buy Rx) = addressable patients; patients x price/injection x injections/year = annual market $; market $ x Botox share = Botox revenue
steps: % severe / willing to buy Rx: 50% → 60M x 0.50 = 30M patients
Injections per year: 1 per 2 months x 12 months = 6 injections/year
Botox potential annual revenue: $36B x 20% = $7.2B (low) to $36B x 40% = $14.4B (high)
math.answer: Total US prescription migraine market: ~$36B/year. Botox potential annual revenue at 20%–40% share: ~$7B–$14B/year.

questions.prompt: Is the market financially attractive given the cost structure?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare the revenue opportunity to the cost base. Development/launch costs are $5B (one-time), annual marketing is $1B, and manufacturing marginal costs are negligible. Even at the low end ($7B/year revenue), the market looks very attractive. Candidate should note that profitability analysis would require a full multi-year model, but the headline numbers are compelling.

math.setup: Revenue vs. costs: annual revenue minus annual marketing cost; compare to $5B upfront investment
steps: Payback period at low end: ~$5B / $6B ≈ <1 year
math.answer: The market is highly attractive. Even at the low revenue estimate, the annual contribution margin covers the full upfront investment in under one year.

questions.prompt: What are the key considerations and risks the client should address before and during the launch?
questions.guidance: Candidate should organize considerations into logical buckets. Strong candidates surface branding/cannibalization risk unprompted. Key areas: Branding risk (Botox brand carries a cosmetic/controversial image; shared brand name exposes both products to adverse event risk), Cannibalization/price erosion (a lower-priced Rx migraine product could drive off-label use and erode the cosmetic segment pricing), Competition and reimbursement (comparable efficacy to generics may make it hard to get insurance formulary placement; many patients cannot afford out-of-pocket), Regulatory (FDA may require different labeling, restrict to certain specialties, mandate separate marketing), Patient/physician behavior (patients are averse to injectable therapies when oral options are available).

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key considerations the client should take into account when deciding how to launch this product?

categories.name: Branding
ideas: The Botox brand carries a cosmetic and somewhat controversial image that may reduce patient willingness to use it for a medical indication
Keeping both products under the same brand name increases risk exposure if a new side effect is discovered for either product
Launching under a separate brand name could help differentiate the two uses and allow independent pricing, but may reduce brand recognition and market traction

categories.name: Cannibalization and Price Erosion
ideas: If physicians and consumers identify that the migraine and cosmetic products are essentially the same compound, it will be very difficult to preserve two separate markets
Launching at a significantly lower price for the migraine indication could drive off-label cosmetic use, eroding pricing and margins in the existing cosmetic segment
The client should investigate regulatory and contractual mechanisms to keep the markets separate

categories.name: Competition and Reimbursement
ideas: The branded oral prescription competitor recently lost patent protection, creating a strong generic alternative
Comparable efficacy to generics may deter insurance companies from adding Botox to formulary
Many migraine sufferers may be unable to afford the $200/injection price out-of-pocket if not covered by insurance

categories.name: Regulatory
ideas: FDA approval is still pending; commercial plans are contingent on successful approval
The FDA may require different labeling and may restrict the indication to certain specialties
Separate marketing campaigns may be required by regulation for each indication

categories.name: Patient and Physician Adoption
ideas: Patients are generally averse to injectable therapies when comparable oral alternatives exist
Physicians in neurology/headache medicine may need significant education and detailing
Strong efficacy data for specific patient subpopulations could support targeted marketing

categories.name: Geographic and Market Expansion
ideas: The client could submit the product for regulatory approval in other countries to expand the addressable market
Targeting specific high-value patient subpopulations (e.g., those with both migraines and cosmetic interest) could maximize uptake

recommendation: The US prescription migraine market is highly attractive, with a potential annual revenue opportunity of $7B–$14B for Botox at a 20%–40% market share — well in excess of the $5B development/launch investment and $1B annual marketing cost
The client should proceed with the launch, but the proposed strategy carries significant risks around cannibalization and branding that must be addressed before commercialization

Launching under a separate brand name is recommended to differentiate the two indications, enable independent pricing, protect the cosmetic franchise from adverse event spillover, and allow targeted marketing to neurologists and migraine patients
risks: Regulatory: The product has not yet received FDA approval; success is contingent on regulatory clearance
Branding: Both same-name and different-name strategies carry risk — reputational issues if same name; lack of market traction if different name
Cannibalization: A lower migraine price point may drive off-label use and erode the cosmetic segment
Reimbursement: Without formulary placement, patient access will be limited given the $200/injection price
Patient aversion: Injectable delivery may suppress adoption relative to oral alternatives
next_steps: Continue clinical trials and secure FDA approval
Set up regulatory, brand, and marketing barriers between the cosmetic and migraine markets
Negotiate contracts with insurance companies and PBMs to secure formulary placement for the migraine indication prior to launch
Evaluate a separate brand name strategy and conduct market research on physician and patient perception
Assess feasibility of international regulatory submissions to expand total addressable market
